  • 探討更年期症狀在歷史文化與現代職場中被「隱形化」的成因，以及高達八成受訪女性工作表現受衝擊的現狀。
  • 比較西班牙的「專項法定假別」與英國的「職場彈性環境調整」等不同應對思維，並借鏡台灣法規進行深度反思。

摘要

從經痛到更年期：女性在職場中難以言說的生理困境

作者以個人擔任駐外記者時必須仰賴強效止痛藥忍受經痛的經歷切入，描述女性步入四、五十歲後，面臨盜汗、失眠、焦慮與腦霧等更年期症狀的折磨。根據歐洲議會研究，約有85%的女性曾出現更年期症狀，更有高達三成屬於會直接影響日常工作的中重度症狀。然而，在以男性視角為主的歷史與醫學發展中，女性停經長期與喪失青春甚至負面標籤連結，導致處於事業成熟期的高階資深女性，往往在職場中對更年期身心轉變保持沉默，進而承受巨大的心理與工作壓力。

西班牙制度革新：正式將更年期嚴重症狀納入病假保障

為正視此一女性生理健康問題，西班牙政府頒布皇家法令，自2023年12月起將更年期病假正式寫入社會安全保障制度。只要經由醫師專業評估，確認症狀已暫時影響工作能力即可開立證明。該制度突破了傳統一般病假的限制，不僅取消了過去五年內須繳納180天社保的門檻，津貼更從請假第二天即開始發放，第2至20天給付60%投保薪資，第21天起增至75%，顯示政府正式肯定更年期造成的實質失能狀態。

法規專項保障與職場彈性調適的兩難抉擇

然而專項假別亦面臨落實挑戰，作者指出西班牙過去推行生理假時，許多女性因害怕被貼上「體弱多病」的標籤而不敢請假，更年期假亦恐引發雇主在招聘與晉升時的職場污名化風險。相較於西班牙的法定專假模式，英國則側重於職場環境調適，鼓勵企業提供彈性工時、改善通風與居家辦公等措施；而台灣雖有無需證明即可請取的生理假，卻未涵蓋停經後的症狀。作者認為相較於訂立難以一體適用的專項病假，推動普遍性的友善彈性工時機制，更能兼顧多元生理需求與工作效率。

I hate getting my period when I'm working. I often have such bad cramps I can't stand up straight, and I break out in a cold sweat. I have to take painkillers, and they have to be the really strong ones prescribed by a doctor, otherwise I can't focus on work at all. Since I'm a foreign correspondent and have no one to cover for me, I can't take menstrual leave, so I always just pop pills and keep working . Around age 45 or 50, my periods started becoming irregular, and my body entered the transition period before menopause. I think I have every menopause symptom in the book: hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia, anxiety. —and what’s most infuriating is that I’ve even gotten dumber. The only comfort is that, well, everyone else goes through it too. According to data compiled by the European Parliamentary Research Service this year, about 85%of women experience at least one menopause-related symptom, with about 25 %to 30%having moderate to severe symptoms that can directly impact their daily life and ability to work. But wait —if you can take menstrual leave when period pain makes it impossible to work.

, shouldn't you also be able to take " menopause leave" when insomnia, hot flashes, and brain fog get so bad that you can't do your job? You can. But you have to live in Spain. Hello everyone, I’m Fan-chi, and welcome to Fan-chi’s View of the World from Taipei. Spain has recently decided to formally write this into their social security system. On October 20th of this year, the Spanish government passed a new royal decree. Starting December 1st. , if a woman’s menopause-related health issues are severe enough to temporarily prevent her from working, a doctor can issue a medical leave certificate. However, you don't get time off just by entering menopause. Applicants must first undergo a medical assessment. A physician must confirm the presence of menopause-related symptoms or conditions that are severe enough to affect work capacity to be eligible. The biggest difference between this and regular sick leave is the social security payment schedule.

Regular sick leave usually only receives social security benefits starting from the fourth day, but the new menopause leave is calculated from the second day . From day two to day 20, you receive 60 %of your insured salary, and from day 21 onwards, it increases to 75%. The threshold required for regular sick leave—having paid social security for at least 180 days in the past five years— has also been removed. Seen in this light, Spain isn't just giving women another type of leave; they are formally acknowledging that menopause can. sometimes be so severe that it truly makes it impossible to work for a while . Since almost every woman goes through menopause, why has it only recently started to be formally included in workplace policy discussions? One reason may be that menopause has long been associated with getting old. Research from Lancaster University in the UK has noted that the image of older women in European history is actually quite complex. Since early times, once a woman lost her fertility, it was often linked to the.

loss of youth, beauty, and femininity. In the past, there were even more extreme portrayals, such as depicting older women as jealous of young girls, or even as threatening witches. By the 18th and 19th centuries, although medicine slowly advanced, the medical system was male-dominated, so the history and treatment of menopause were primarily recorded from their perspective, with women's voices rarely preserved, leading to menopause being treated as a female condition in need of. management. This. Perhaps this also explains why, even now, many people are still reluctant to openly say at work, "My work performance has been poor lately because I'm going through menopause." Furthermore, menopause usually occurs between the ages of 45 and 55. At this age, many women are not ready to retire ; they have accumulated 20 or 30 years of work experience, may be leading teams in management roles, and are often the most experienced people in the company.

Therefore, menopause remains relatively invisible in the workplace, likely not because it affects few people, but. because we have long been unaccustomed to treating it as a topic for open discussion. Spain did not just suddenly think to include menopause in workplace regulations. As early as 2023, Spain became the first European country to include menstrual leave under special medical leave protections, but it is not available just because of a period; it can only be requested for conditions like endometriosis or pelvic inflammatory disease that cause pain so severe it makes working impossible. After the policy was implemented, there.

was no surge in people taking leave. Within the first 11 months of the regulation, only 1,559 instances of menstrual leave were recorded across Spain, averaging fewer than five people per day. Reasons include strict eligibility criteria requiring a doctor's diagnosis, as well as concerns among women that revealing the true reason to their company might lead to being labeled as "constantly sick." So, menopause leave is currently facing the same dilemma. On one hand, some feel that if symptoms truly affect work, the system should be adjusted. On the other, there is concern that by legally singling out women's physical needs, companies might perceive women as being more troublesome. Scholars researching labor and gender policies have noted that while such policies acknowledge the real physiological needs of women, they could also lead to stigmatization, potentially impacting employers 'decisions during hiring or promotions. handling this? The UK currently does not have menopause-specific sick leave either, but officials have shifted their focus to workplace adjustments in recent years. The UK’s Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service suggests that employers offer flexible hours, more breaks, work-from-home options, task adjustments, and improved ventilation or fans. formal sick leave system, while the UK emphasizes adjusting work environments and methods. But is it really a choice between only these two ways to care for women's health needs? The European Parliament is preparing to formally discuss the impact of menopause on women and the broader economy this year, titled "Menopause is Not Just a Health Issue," aiming to make menopause an economic, workplace, and social priority. Although this is currently a report for forming policy positions rather than a. law, it shows that menopause is gradually moving from a purely medical issue to being discussed alongside workplace, economic, and gender equality matters. Taiwan was actually ahead of many European countries regarding menstrual leave. We don’t have to wait for severe pain to be diagnosed as a specific disease to be eligible for leave. Under the Act of Gender Equality in Employment , if women have difficulty working due to their menstrual cycle, they can take one day of menstrual leave per month without a medical certificate. Like sick leave, it is paid; the first three days.

do not count toward the annual sick leave limit, and any subsequent days are calculated as part of regular sick leave . However, when menopause hits, if you're still menstruating and experience difficulty working due to your period, you can take menstrual leave. But after menopause, even if you're uncomfortable from symptoms, menstrual leave no longer applies. Spain's new system prompts us to reflect : as women's bodies change from menstruation and pregnancy to menopause , shouldn't workplace policies evolve as well? If symptoms are severe enough to affect. your work, would you support creating a specific type of medical leave, or would you prefer more flexible working hours and environments for all employees? I personally support the latter, as everyone's physical condition is different and it's hard to set rigid rules. I admit it's tough for managers; even with just remote work at our company, I sometimes worry about potential drops in efficiency. Thanks to in5 for today. 作者以個人擔任駐外記者時必須仰賴強效止痛藥忍受經痛的經歷切入，描述女性步入四、五十歲後，面臨盜汗、失眠、焦慮與腦霧等更年期症狀的折磨。根據歐洲議會研究，約有85%的女性曾出現更年期症狀，更有高達三成屬於會直接影響日常工作的中重度症狀。然而，在以男性視角為主的歷史與醫學發展中，女性停經長期與喪失青春甚至負面標籤連結，導致處於事業成熟期的高階資深女性，往往在職場中對更年期身心轉變保持沉默，進而承受巨大的心理與工作壓力。

西班牙制度革新：正式將更年期嚴重症狀納入病假保障

為正視此一女性生理健康問題，西班牙政府頒布皇家法令，自2023年12月起將更年期病假正式寫入社會安全保障制度。只要經由醫師專業評估，確認症狀已暫時影響工作能力即可開立證明。該制度突破了傳統一般病假的限制，不僅取消了過去五年內須繳納180天社保的門檻，津貼更從請假第二天即開始發放，第2至20天給付60%投保薪資，第21天起增至75%，顯示政府正式肯定更年期造成的實質失能狀態。

法規專項保障與職場彈性調適的兩難抉擇

然而專項假別亦面臨落實挑戰，作者指出西班牙過去推行生理假時，許多女性因害怕被貼上「體弱多病」的標籤而不敢請假，更年期假亦恐引發雇主在招聘與晉升時的職場污名化風險。相較於西班牙的法定專假模式，英國則側重於職場環境調適，鼓勵企業提供彈性工時、改善通風與居家辦公等措施；而台灣雖有無需證明即可請取的生理假，卻未涵蓋停經後的症狀。作者認為相較於訂立難以一體適用的專項病假，推動普遍性的友善彈性工時機制，更能兼顧多元生理需求與工作效率。

摘要

危機中的接班人選

作者介紹，輝達財務長柯萊特・克瑞斯據稱受命擔任公司臨時執行長，外界因此關注她能否接下黃仁勳留下的重任。彭博分析指出，企業遭逢危機時，董事會常由財務長暫時掌舵：財務長熟悉公司狀況，也與投資人、銀行及客戶往來，較能傳遞「公司仍然穩定」的訊息。克瑞斯在輝達任職十三年，熟悉營運各面向，分析人士形容她如同公司的瑞士刀，實際職責也接近營運長。

低調務實的風格與危機考驗

克瑞斯的作風與擅長站上舞台、談論未來願景的黃仁勳大不相同。她行事低調、發言謹慎，熟識她的人則認為她務實、冷靜，必要時也敢對黃仁勳說「不」。不過，她在輝達的職涯並非一路順遂。2018年，加密貨幣價格下跌，礦工停止採購顯示卡，通路商因此囤積大量庫存。公司原先預期庫存會迅速消化，實際復甦速度卻比預想緩慢；輝達宣布下一季營收將大幅低於市場預期後，股價兩天內重挫逾28%，克瑞斯與黃仁勳也遭股東訴訟指控未充分揭露挖礦需求對營收的影響。這場風波讓克瑞斯必須同時處理財務壓力與市場信心崩落。

從財務專業走進輝達

克瑞斯現年59歲，並非工程師或公司創辦人，而是長年深耕科技業財務管理的專業人士。她在亞利桑那大學攻讀金融並取得MBA，先後於德州儀器、微軟及思科任職，累積近25年的科技業財務管理經驗。2013年，46歲的她已在思科擔任高階主管，生活與工作相對穩定；當時規模遠不如微軟、思科的輝達，主要以遊戲顯示卡聞名。她的兩個兒子熱愛電玩，知道輝達顯示卡的實力，便鼓勵母親接受邀請。真正說服她的則是黃仁勳：他以白板描繪人工智慧的未來，指出原本用於遊戲的GPU終有一天會成為AI的重要基礎。

公司文化與財富累積

克瑞斯也重視企業文化，認為留住人才不只靠加薪。她主張領導者應聆聽各階層員工的意見，讓最了解專案的人能發揮影響力，不因職稱高低而被忽略，也應營造持續學習新技能的環境。影片並提到，隨著輝達股價與公司價值攀升，她持有的公司股票大幅增值；報導援引《富比士》估算，她的身家達12億美元，躋身美國富有的白手起家女性之列。

「玻璃懸崖」與領導挑戰

克瑞斯在公司動盪時接掌重任，也引發外界對「玻璃懸崖」的討論。這個概念指女性往往在組織陷入危機時才獲得高階職位，接下成功機率較低、失敗風險較高的任務；若未能扭轉局勢，外界又可能將結果歸咎於女性不適合領導。影片以雅虎前執行長瑪麗莎・梅爾、前美國副總統賀錦麗及英國前首相特拉斯等案例，說明女性與少數族群有時會在局勢不利時承擔重任。作者提醒，玻璃懸崖並不代表女性注定失敗；克瑞斯能否成功，除了取決於她的領導能力，也取決於董事會願意給予多少權力與支持。影片最後邀請觀眾討論，沒有黃仁勳的輝達能否繼續發光。

If your child told you, "Mom, you should go work for that video game chip company ," would you listen? Bloomberg analyzes that this is actually a typical approach for American companies when facing a crisis. When a company suddenly runs into trouble and needs someone to take the helm, the board often turns to the CFO, because the CFO not only. understands the company's financial status best but also regularly deals with investors, banks, and clients, giving them the credibility and network to stabilize the situation during chaos . A U.S. corporate executive told Bloomberg that in times of crisis, a CFO is often the most suitable interim leader, because at such times, the company doesn't need grand visions, but rather the message: "We are still stable ; there is no need to panic." And Colette is no ordinary CFO; she has been at NVIDIA for 13 years, which is more than double the average tenure for a CFO at a major U.S. corporation. Tech.

analysts describe her as someone indispensable to everything Jensen does ; she is like NVIDIA’s Swiss Army knife , able to handle anything, and her actual role is closer to that of an COO . Interestingly, her personality is almost the polar opposite of Jensen Huang’s. Jensen loves wearing his signature leather jacket, giving speeches about the future, and carrying a star aura, while Colette is extremely low-profile, rarely seeks the spotlight , and is always cautious with her public statements; however, those who know her describe her as incredibly pragmatic, calm, and thoughtful, and she isn't afraid to say "no" to Jensen when necessary. However, it hasn't always been smooth sailing for Colette at. NVIDIA; in 2018, she faced one of the most severe crises of her tenure: the crypto mining crash. You might recall that back then, Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies were surging. Miners everywhere were snapping up NVIDIA graphics cards for mining, causing company profits to soar, but when coin prices crashed, miners suddenly stopped buying, leaving distributors' warehouses piled high with unsold cards. That November, Kress admitted at an earnings call that the company had expected the inventory to clear quickly. Things didn't go as planned; the market recovered slower than expected. When they announced that next-quarter revenue would fall far short of market expectations, the stock plummeted over 28%in two days, leading to shareholder lawsuits naming Kress and Jensen Huang as defendants for failing to disclose the impact of mining on revenue. This crisis showed that even a tech giant like NVIDIA could severely misjudge market demand, and as CFO, Kress had to not only manage the company's finances but also navigate a collapse in market confidence.

Stand firm. At 59, Kress differs from Jensen Huang in that she is neither an engineer nor a founder; she has spent half her life managing finances at tech companies. She studied finance at the University of Arizona and later earned an MBA. Her first long-term role was at Texas Instruments, followed by 13 years at Microsoft, where she served as CFO for the Server and Tools division, before moving to Cisco in 2010 as a senior VP and divisional CFO. Simply put, she has accumulated nearly. 25 years of financial management experience in the tech industry. The turning point in her life came in 2013. At 46, she was already a senior executive at Cisco with a stable career when Jensen Huang came to recruit her as NVIDIA's CFO. However, NVIDIA was much smaller back then compared to giants like Microsoft or Cisco, focusing primarily on graphics cards, with gaming GPUs being their most well-known product . While she was hesitant, two career advisors appeared at home: her then eight and ten-year-old sons. Kress told Bloomberg that her sons loved gaming and already knew how powerful NVIDIA's graphics cards were, so they encouraged their mother to join the company. Of course, while the kids ' advice was one thing, it was Jensen Huang who truly convinced her. Huang personally walked her through NVIDIA's future plans, even using a whiteboard to sketch out his vision for the AI industry. At the time, when people thought of NVIDIA, they only thought of gaming and pretty 3D graphics, but Huang convinced her otherwise. He argued that the GPUs originally used for gaming would one day become the essential foundation for AI, which is why Kress.

decided to accept the challenge. She also places great importance on the company's culture, believing that retaining talent requires more than just raises. Beyond a comprehensive benefits system, he emphasized in an interview with Fortune that good leaders should be willing to listen to employees at all levels, not just those in the highest positions. He said that at Quora, the organization is relatively flat; if you are the one who understands a project best, the company should listen to your input regardless of your job title, while also fostering an environment where employees. learn new skills and knowledge every day . Over 13 years, thanks to her Quora stock , Forbes estimates D'Angelo's net worth reached $ 1.2 billion this June, making her one of America's wealthiest self-made women. Ranked 32nd on the list, this job. Not only changed her life but also her bank. However, as she steps in to put out the fire, some foreign media have begun to discuss the "glass cliff" phenomenon. You may have heard of the "glass ceiling. ," which refers to the invisible barriers women often encounter; the " glass cliff" is a concept proposed by British scholars in 2005, where women finally reach high-level positions just as a company enters a crisis, the moment they are most likely to fail. Subsequent studies found that minorities face similar situations, most notably. The famous case of Yahoo hiring former Google executive Marissa Mayer as CEO in 2012, though Yahoo had long been beaten by Google by then. She worked hard to reform the company for five years, but in the end, its core business was sold.

to Verizon. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 從男性精子品質、女性凍卵到胚胎基因篩選，了解科技如何改變生育準備與選擇。
  • 拆解多基因胚胎篩檢的原理、商業推力與科學限制，避免把預測結果誤當成確定答案。
  • 透過當事父母與作者的經歷，看見生育科技背後的焦慮、倫理爭議與漫長等待。

摘要

生育焦慮與「卵子最大化」

台灣生育率低迷，不只反映有人選擇不生，也掩蓋了許多人想要孩子、卻難以順利懷孕的處境。有人尋求試管嬰兒、捐卵或捐精，也有人跨國尋找代理孕母；而在美國矽谷，部分人更試圖把生育推向極限，想在胚胎植入前比較基因，挑選理想中的孩子。

三十歲的康納得知妻子自然受孕不易後，開始研究如何改善精子品質，少喝酒、改穿寬鬆內褲、避免手機放在口袋，並服用營養補充品。網路上甚至有人以冰水浸泡睪丸，希望增加精子生成；但即使後來成功懷孕，也難以確認究竟是哪種方法發揮作用。與此同時，矽谷一個名為「Egg Rolling」的女性社群，成員致力於反覆取卵、累積數十甚至數百顆卵子，這種做法被稱為「卵子最大化」，有些人希望藉此保留生育機會，有些人則想日後培養更多胚胎並進行基因篩選。

胚胎也能像商品一樣比較？

這些準備背後有現實因素：研究估計，全球男性平均精子濃度在1973至2018年間下降約52%；女性的卵子儲備則會隨年齡增加而減少，卵子染色體異常的機率也會上升。晚婚晚育日益普遍，使不少女性希望趁年輕多保存卵子。

《紐約》雜誌報導的亞瑟與查斯，計畫透過捐卵及代理孕母生育，並使用基因公司 Genomic Prediction 評估胚胎未來的智商、身高，以及心臟病、糖尿病等疾病風險，服務費用高達約新台幣164萬元。他們從30顆成熟卵子開始，經過培養與檢測，最後留下三個染色體正常的胚胎。由於預測的智商與身高差異不大，兩人主要依據疾病風險作出選擇。生孩子似乎從祈求平安出生，變成能逐項比較條件的決策。

技術進步、商業化與生育觀念

胚胎篩選熱潮有三個推力。第一是基因技術進步：傳統胚胎著床前檢測能檢查特定遺傳疾病或染色體異常；新興的多基因胚胎篩檢則利用大型基因資料庫與統計模型，估算多種基因變異與疾病風險、身高等特徵的關聯。Genomic Prediction 會提供胚胎比較報告，Nucleus Genomics 甚至設計出類似網購介面的工具，讓使用者排序不同特徵。

第二是生殖醫療逐漸成為高價、客製化服務。Genomic Prediction 曾在紐約地鐵刊登「打造最好的寶寶」廣告，並吸引約三千人登記等候。部分父母不願把孩子的健康交給運氣，希望取得更多基因資訊；若未來能以人體細胞在實驗室大量製造卵子，可供篩選的胚胎還可能更多。

第三是生育理念的轉變。矽谷的鼓勵生育思潮常強調傳承優良基因，但不少父母並非想生很多孩子，而是認為既然能用科技降低疾病風險，就值得一試。只是降低遺傳疾病風險與挑選智商、身高或壽命，牽涉不同層次的倫理問題。哈佛醫學院調查中，77%受訪者支持以胚胎篩檢降低特定身體疾病風險，支持藉此選擇身體特徵者則約為30%，顯示多數人追求的未必是完美寶寶。

預測的限制與父母的焦慮

多基因篩檢的效果仍有爭議。美國生殖醫學會指出，目前證據不足以證明這項技術具有可靠的臨床效益，因此不建議作為常規醫療服務。Genomic Prediction 曾宣稱經篩選的胚胎智商預測差距可能達九分，但這個比較前提是至少有20個可用胚胎；許多接受試管療程的父母，最後往往只有一兩個胚胎可供選擇。研究者也提醒，預測存在誤差，而不同多基因分數可能選出不同的「最佳」胚胎。科技公司所說的「最好」，並沒有科學界一致認定的標準。

然而，父母的焦慮是真實的。父親麥克斯與伴侶進行試管療程後，只得到兩個可用胚胎，基因分析顯示兩者預測壽命僅差五個月，他們仍決定再次接受療程，盼望有更多選擇。亞瑟的兒子出生後，他也因讀到高海拔環境可能影響神經發展的研究而擔憂，甚至考慮改變居住安排。

作者也分享了自身經驗：他們透過美國代理孕母迎來 Amo，從捐卵、試管嬰兒到胚胎篩檢，最後留下四個胚胎，並依基因檢測結果排序。然而，他們認為最理想的胚胎並未成功著床；歷經多次失敗，四年後才終於迎接孩子。這段經歷讓作者體會到，生殖科技能提供大量資訊，卻不能保證懷孕成功，也無法消除等待與不確定性。

================================================

It’s no longer news that Taiwan has the world's lowest fertility rate. While choosing not to have children is a personal decision, beyond economic issues, the low fertility rate also masks the reality that many people want to have children but are unable to do so successfully. Some people constantly seek help from in vitro fertilization and other assisted reproductive technologies to have children; some need egg donors or sperm donors, and others even have to cross borders to find surrogates to realize their dream of becoming parents. However, a more surprising trend has emerged in Silicon Valley, USA. There is a group of people who not only want to use technology to have children but also want to push their reproductive. capabilities to the limit, even hoping to compare and grade the genes of their future babies before deciding which one to choose. So, do they really get their wish and have a perfect baby? From high-tech gadgets to major revolutions, how particular are we about having children and conception today? There was a 30- year-old man, Connor, whose wife struggled to conceive for over a year. The doctor told him that natural conception was likely difficult. Connor was devastated upon hearing this and began obsessively researching how to improve the quality of his sperm and maximize his fertility. He started.

drinking less alcohol, switched to loose-fitting underwear, stopped keeping his phone in his pocket, and took various nutritional supplements. Online , some people even soak their testicles in ice water every day, believing it helps with sperm production. Some of these methods have scientific backing, while others do not. Even if Connor later successfully helped his wife conceive, there is no way to determine which measure actually worked. Women are not far behind. An investigation by The Information reporter this year found that there is a women's group in Silicon Valley called "Egg Rolling," with over 80 members, many of whom are high-level. tech professionals. What they study isn't how to "freeze eggs," but how to accumulate hundreds or even 200 eggs through repeated retrievals; this trend is called "egg maximization." Some women just want to preserve their future fertility, but others hope to create more embryos in the future and then use genetic technology to select the "ideal" one. It is actually quite common to spend so much energy on preparing for pregnancy. A study published in 2021 found that in the 45 years leading up to 2018, the average global male sperm concentration fell by.

an estimated 52%. Another Danish study also found that while the quantity of sperm from local donors did not decrease significantly, the total number of motile sperm dropped by 22%over three years. For women, the issue is more practical. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists points out that a woman's egg reserve steadily declines from birth, and as she gets older, the likelihood of chromosomal abnormalities in her eggs increases. Especially now that more and more people are marrying and having children later, it’s no wonder many women want to freeze more eggs while they are young to preserve their chances of having children in the future. Once the eggs. are ready, the next step is to maximize the embryos themselves. A couple interviewed by New York magazine this year, Arthur and Chas, did exactly that. Arthur, who previously worked at tech companies like Amazon and Twitter, is a massive data enthusiast. They hoped to have their own child through egg donation and a surrogate, but Arthur wanted to go further by using a company called Genomic Prediction to analyze the embryo’s future IQ, height, and risks for diseases like heart disease and diabetes. This service costs as much as 1.64 million New Taiwan Dollars. Starting with 30 mature eggs,.

they went through cultivation and testing, eventually leaving three embryos with normal chromosomes for further comparison. The predicted IQ and height for the three embryos were actually quite similar, so they ultimately based their choice mainly on disease risk. In the past, having a baby meant just hoping for a safe delivery, but now you can actually compare various criteria like shopping for goods; how exactly is this technology achieving this? And why are more and more people wanting to use it? There are three key drivers behind this wave of embryo maximization. , the first being the obvious advancement in genetic technology. With IVF in the past, doctors could use pre-implantation genetic testing to check for specific hereditary diseases or abnormal chromosome counts; for example, some severe single-gene disorders could be avoided with testing to help parents. Now, a technique called polygenic embryo screening has emerged. The concept is simple: conditions like diabetes, heart disease, or even height aren't determined by a single gene, but are influenced by many genes and environmental factors. So, scientists use large genetic databases to analyze.

the relationship between different genetic variants and diseases, then use statistical models to score embryos and predict their likely future traits and higher disease risks. Genomic Prediction can organize the genetic information of different embryos into a report for parents to compare. The magazine also discovered that another company, Nucleus Genomics, has even launched an interface that allows you to sort through various embryo traits, much like shopping for items online. The second driver is that reproductive medicine is starting to become a premium, customized commodity. Last year, Genomic Prediction ran large. advertisements in the New York subway boldly declaring, "Create your best baby ." Even though it sparked controversy, the result was that about 3,000 people signed up for the waitlist. Why are so many people willing to spend the money? A lab director at Genomic Prediction told NPR that some parents simply don't want to leave their child's health to chance and want as much genetic information as possible. Moreover, there is still significant room for this business to grow. If, in the future, scientists can truly mass-produce eggs in the lab using human cells, parents might not need to go through repeated egg retrievals and could obtain more.

embryos to screen. The third driver is a change in the philosophy of having children. We previously introduced the pro-natalism popular in Silicon Valley, where people like Elon Musk believe that superior genes should be passed on through more children. However, many parents don't want to have a dozen kids ; they just think if technology can reduce the risk of disease, why not give it a try? These two ways of thinking might seem similar, but they are actually backed by very different values . Using technology to reduce the risk of hereditary disease versus choosing a child's IQ, height, or lifespan are ethical issues on different levels. A poll by the Harvard Medical School found. that 77%of respondents support using embryo screening to reduce the risk of certain physical diseases. However, only about 30%of people support using it to select physical traits. This means that most people don't necessarily want a perfect baby; they just hope their children are... No. However, a major problem arises here : when tech companies tell you that spending money can result in a smarter, healthier child, are these predictions actually that accurate? First, it must be said that genetic testing does have.

significant medical value, especially for parents with a history of hereditary diseases; these technologies can help them lower the risk of having a child with a serious condition. But the efficacy of polygenic embryo screening remains highly controversial. The American Society for Reproductive Medicine clearly stated late last year that there is currently insufficient evidence to prove that this new screening technology has reliable clinical benefits, and therefore, it is not recommended as a routine medical service. New York Magazine also revealed that Genomic Prediction once claimed that the predicted IQ difference between screened embryos could be as much as nine points. However, that 前提 is that。you must first have 20 usable embryos to compare the highest and lowest scores. The problem is that many parents doing IVF end up with only one or two viable embryos. Geneticists point out that even with one embryo, the actual benefits of this technology may be limited, and the predictions themselves have margins of error. A 2024 study published in a Nature-affiliated journal found that using different polygenic scores can even result in selecting different " best" embryos due to varying criteria. So, if a tech company tells you they can use an algorithm to select the best baby , don't rush to pay up, because even scientists might not have a consensus on.

what "the best" actually means. However , what I think is worth considering is the genuine anxiety felt by these parents. Wired magazine interviewed a father named Max, who, after undergoing IVF with his partner, only ended up with two viable embryos. Genetic analysis showed a difference of only five months in predicted lifespan between the two, so they decided to go through IVF again , hoping for more options. As for Arthur , mentioned at the beginning, he was still worried after his son was born because he read a study suggesting that high-altitude environments might affect a child’s neurological development, and. he even considered changing the family’s living arrangements. This reminds me of our own experience. We welcomed Amo’s birth through surrogacy in the U.S. After egg donation, IVF, and embryo screening, we were left with four embryos. These embryos were ranked after genetic testing, but the one we thought was the best didn't result in a successful pregnancy. After several failures, it took us four years to finally welcome our child. This experience made me deeply realize that reproductive technology can provide a lot of information and help parents make choices, but it cannot guarantee.

the outcome. Of course, we want our children to be healthy, to have fewer illnesses and more opportunities—a sentiment every parent can understand— but that doesn’t mean we can truly use technology to determine who our children will become in the future. A science journalist interviewed by Vox reminded us that becoming a parent is fundamentally a process of learning to let go of control. Human genetics are too complex, and no matter how advanced technology becomes, it cannot dictate a child's entire life. Returning to Taiwan , beyond discussing how to increase birth rates, we should also look at whether those who want children but cannot conceive have sufficient medical. resources and institutional support. For some, having a child is a wish that can only be realized after a long and arduous journey. Whether it's IVF, donation, or surrogacy, different ways of having children shouldn't be seen as abnormal or unworthy of support just because they don't fit the traditional family mold. Technology should help us expand the possibilities of becoming parents, rather than ensuring that only the wealthy can access good reproductive choices. But we must remember that a child is not an investment, nor is a human being a product whose return on investment can be calculated. We can strive to give our children a better start in life, but we cannot demand that.

their lives conform to our predetermined standards. If one day you could pay to learn more about your child’s genetic information before they are born, how much would you want to know, and what price would you be willing to pay for such uncertainty? Feel free to leave your comments and share your thoughts. Great. Revolution.

The concept is simple: conditions like diabetes, heart disease, or even height aren't determined by a single gene, but are influenced by many genes and environmental factors. So, scientists use large genetic databases to analyze.

the relationship between different genetic variants and diseases, then use statistical models to score embryos and predict their likely future traits and higher disease risks. Genomic Prediction can organize the genetic information of different embryos into a report for parents to compare. The magazine also discovered that another company, Nucleus Genomics, has even launched an interface that allows you to sort through various embryo traits, much like shopping for items online. The second driver is that reproductive medicine is starting to become a premium, customized commodity. Last year, Genomic Prediction ran large. advertisements in the New York subway boldly declaring, "Create your best baby ." Even though it sparked controversy, the result was that about 3,000 people signed up for the waitlist. Why are so many people willing to spend the money? A lab director at Genomic Prediction told NPR that some parents simply don't want to leave their child's health to chance and want as much genetic information as possible. Moreover, there is still significant room for this business to grow. If, in the future, scientists can truly mass-produce eggs in the lab using human cells, parents might not need to go through repeated egg retrievals and could obtain more.

embryos to screen. The third driver is a change in the philosophy of having children. We previously introduced the pro-natalism popular in Silicon Valley, where people like Elon Musk believe that superior genes should be passed on through more children. However, many parents don't want to have a dozen kids ; they just think if technology can reduce the risk of disease, why not give it a try? These two ways of thinking might seem similar, but they are actually backed by very different values . Using technology to reduce the risk of hereditary disease versus choosing a child's IQ, height, or lifespan are ethical issues on different levels. A poll by the Harvard Medical School found. that 77%of respondents support using embryo screening to reduce the risk of certain physical diseases. However, only about 30%of people support using it to select physical traits. This means that most people don't necessarily want a perfect baby; they just hope their children are... No. However, a major problem arises here : when tech companies tell you that spending money can result in a smarter, healthier child, are these predictions actually that accurate? First, it must be said that genetic testing does have.

significant medical value, especially for parents with a history of hereditary diseases; these technologies can help them lower the risk of having a child with a serious condition. But the efficacy of polygenic embryo screening remains highly controversial. The American Society for Reproductive Medicine clearly stated late last year that there is currently insufficient evidence to prove that this new screening technology has reliable clinical benefits, and therefore, it is not recommended as a routine medical service. New York Magazine also revealed that Genomic Prediction once claimed that the predicted IQ difference between screened embryos could be as much as nine points. Geneticists point out that even with one embryo, the actual benefits of this technology may be limited, and the predictions themselves have margins of error. A 2024 study published in a Nature-affiliated journal found that using different polygenic scores can even result in selecting different " best" embryos due to varying criteria. So, if a tech company tells you they can use an algorithm to select the best baby , don't rush to pay up, because even scientists might not have a consensus on.

what "the best" actually means. However , what I think is worth considering is the genuine anxiety felt by these parents. Wired magazine interviewed a father named Max, who, after undergoing IVF with his partner, only ended up with two viable embryos. Genetic analysis showed a difference of only five months in predicted lifespan between the two, so they decided to go through IVF again , hoping for more options. As for Arthur , mentioned at the beginning, he was still worried after his son was born because he read a study suggesting that high-altitude environments might affect a child’s neurological development, and. he even considered changing the family’s living arrangements. This reminds me of our own experience. We welcomed Amo’s birth through surrogacy in the U.S. After egg donation, IVF, and embryo screening, we were left with four embryos. These embryos were ranked after genetic testing, but the one we thought was the best didn't result in a successful pregnancy. After several failures, it took us four years to finally welcome our child. This experience made me deeply realize that reproductive technology can provide a lot of information and help parents make choices, but it cannot guarantee.

the outcome. Of course, we want our children to be healthy, to have fewer illnesses and more opportunities—a sentiment every parent can understand— but that doesn’t mean we can truly use technology to determine who our children will become in the future. A science journalist interviewed by Vox reminded us that becoming a parent is fundamentally a process of learning to let go of control. Human genetics are too complex, and no matter how advanced technology becomes, it cannot dictate a child's entire life. Returning to Taiwan , beyond discussing how to increase birth rates, we should also look at whether those who want children but cannot conceive have sufficient medical. resources and institutional support. For some, having a child is a wish that can only be realized after a long and arduous journey. Whether it's IVF, donation, or surrogacy, different ways of having children shouldn't be seen as abnormal or unworthy of support just because they don't fit the traditional family mold. Technology should help us expand the possibilities of becoming parents, rather than ensuring that only the wealthy can access good reproductive choices. But we must remember that a child is not an investment, nor is a human being a product whose return on investment can be calculated. We can strive to give our children a better start in life, but we cannot demand that.

their lives conform to our predetermined standards.
